engagement_title: Cascadia Founders Summit: eighteen self-submitted portraits brought to one credible house treatment, cut to the crops the programme and the stage need, bound into the venue printer's badge artwork as a live run, and carried into the programme and announcement set
vertical: Party, events and promotion: a paid professional founders summit in Portland, Oregon, with delegate passes at 600 to 1,200 dollars and an audience of founders, operators and institutional investors
real_brief_anchor: Two ledger anchors, both Freelancer.com. The first, 'Traditional Corporate Headshot Session Needed', whose grounding_note describes 'classic/formal corporate head-shots, neutral light-grey backdrop, colour + clean black-and-white versions, deliverables for social-profile/company website/print, one-week turnaround'. The second, a corporate-website retouch open call quoted verbatim in its grounding_note: 'professionally enhance a complete set of images for our corporate website', 'correct lighting imbalances and exposure issues', 'create a consistent visual style across all website images', 'showcase our facilities, operations, equipment and people', 'maintain a natural and realistic appearance'. Absorbs AO-104 and AO-20. The rebuild is needed because both absorbed tasks sat on a single surface and both ended in a set of crops, which is one deliverable, not four. The fuller commission an events client of this shape actually posts is the one here: the portraits are only useful once they are bound into the badge run the venue printer will actually print and into the programme and announcement collateral, and it is in the binding that a badly prepared crop stops being invisible. All names in the legacy grounding notes are discarded and replaced: the summit, its fourteen speakers and its four staff are invented and Western or European throughout (Marguerite Halloran, Peter Vance, Ines Moreau, Anders Lindqvist, Colm Byrne, Dana Whitfield, Estelle Rioux, Grant Mackey, Sofia Bellini, Nils Haugen, Robin Tate, Bernadette Cruz, Hugo Almeida, Karin Voss, plus staff Laurel Beckett, Owen Faraday, Mireille Dufort and Jonah Pryce).
client_one_liner: Every speaker sent a headshot taken somewhere different, our own team's photos are worse, and the badges have to be at the printer in nine days.
client_brief:
Cascadia Founders Summit, Portland, second edition.

We run a two-day summit for founders and the people who fund them. Passes are six hundred to twelve hundred dollars and the room is about four hundred people. We are nine days from the badge deadline and we have a problem with pictures.

We have fourteen speakers and four of our own team. Every speaker sent whatever headshot they had. One is from a magazine shoot, two came from their PR agency and look it, several were taken in an office with whatever light was in the room, and a couple are cropped so tightly you can barely get a square out of them. Our own four are worse. Put them next to each other and it looks like eighteen different events.

What we need is for all eighteen to look like they belong to the same summit. Understated and credible, the way a serious professional event looks. Not glamour retouching, not that flat direct-flash look, and please do not make anyone look like a different person. Our audience pays to be in the room and they read the calibre of the event off things like this.

We need the pictures at the shapes we actually use: the portrait shape that runs in the printed programme, a tight square for badges and avatars, and a wide one for the lower third of the stage screens. Each person needs to sit on our house ground rather than whatever room they were photographed in, and for the stage screens we need them without any ground at all so our AV team can drop them over the session video.

The badges are the urgent piece. Our venue printer ran our badges last year and we are using the same artwork, but we only have the file they sent us, not whatever it was made from. Each badge carries the person's name, their role line and their affiliation, plus their picture. The speaker list is attached the way our registration system exported it. The role lines are how the speakers wrote them and how their contracts say they print, so they go on as written.

We build our own website, so we do not need pages. What we do need is the printed programme's opening page, a title slide the stage team can restyle per session, and a square announcement we post when each speaker is confirmed. Those three in one file we can edit ourselves, please, because we confirm speakers weekly.

One more thing. The venue has not opened yet so nobody has a photograph of it. We have the architect's render but it looks like a render. If you think the programme opener needs a real picture, get one.

What we need back: the eighteen at all three shapes plus the no-ground versions, the badges ready for the printer and one file per person named so registration can reprint a single badge without opening it, the three canvases as one editable file with its source, a board our team can review from, and a note on what you did to each portrait and what type we are now using.
price_band_and_audience: Delegate passes 600 to 1,200 dollars, two days, roughly four hundred attendees, speakers who are founders, operators and institutional investors, audience aged 28 to 55 who expense the ticket. The band is load-bearing. At this level the portraiture has to be understated, even and credible: neutral house ground, natural skin, no visible retouching signature, one consistent scale of head in frame across eighteen people so the programme grid reads as one event. Push it toward glamour retouching, smoothed skin, bright eyes and a warm glossy finish, and it reads as a consumer conference selling to the wrong buyer. Leave it flat and hard-lit and it reads as a free meetup. The programme and the announcement set follow the same rule: generous white space, restrained type, one strong photograph, and the summit's mark used quietly. An agent that ships either extreme has misread the commission even if every crop is dimensionally correct. A posted job of this shape runs 1,500 to 3,000 dollars fixed on a nine-day turnaround.

brand_identity.brand_assets_status: The summit builds its own website and needs no pages. Its badge artwork exists only as the press PDF the venue printer ran last year, with no working file behind it. The house ground, mark and tone are described in the brand notes rather than handed over as a kit.
brand_identity.values: A serious room worth the price of admission, where credibility is read off the smallest details.

assets_supplied.name: speaker_portraits/ (14 files) and staff_portraits/ (4 files)
assets_supplied.visible_description: "Everything we were sent. Fourteen speakers, four of our own team. Different rooms, different light, different everything." Mixed dimensions from roughly 1,100px to 5,600px on the long edge, all head-and-shoulders, Western and European sitters, no two grounds alike.
assets_supplied.hidden_defect: Two things nobody at the summit can see. First, three of the fourteen speaker frames are cropped so tightly at the top that the wide stage-screen shape cannot be derived from them without either clipping the crown of the head or inventing pixels, and the crop tool answers that with a tradeoff rather than a refusal and will interpolate toward its cap while reporting it only in a metadata entry. The only route that does not invent pixels is to add material at the edges first, and whether the added band actually matches that sitter's own ground and the house treatment is a property of that frame that cannot be known before it is done. Second, two of the frames arrived already heavily retouched by an agency, with skin smoothed and eyes lifted, so bringing them to the house treatment makes them read plastic beside the sixteen untouched ones rather than bringing them into line.

assets_supplied.name: summit_badge_2025_PRINTER.pdf
assets_supplied.visible_description: "The badge artwork our venue printer ran last year. We only have what they sent us." A real press PDF at 100 x 70 mm portrait, fonts embedded, produced from a genuine page layout. Carries the name, the role line, the affiliation, the summit mark and the person's picture.
assets_supplied.hidden_defect: The printed badge reads as a square picture chip, but the graphic frame behind it is a tall portrait rectangle at roughly three to four, and the frame fits whatever is bound into it on its own terms. A square badge crop bound into it is fitted to the frame's proportion and the crown of the head is cut on every single record, silently, with the merge reporting success and every badge looking deliberate in isolation. The frame's proportion is geometry inherited from a printer nobody at the summit can ask. On the text side the name and the role line share one continuous story while the affiliation sits alone, so the fields cannot be addressed uniformly.

assets_supplied.name: speakers.csv
assets_supplied.visible_description: "The speaker list as our registration system exported it. Role lines print as written, that is in the contracts." Columns for name, role line, affiliation, session and a photo filename.
assets_supplied.hidden_defect: Twenty rows for eighteen people: two speakers registered twice, once through the speaker portal and once through the general registration, with different affiliations on each row. Headers are mixed-case with trailing spaces and the photo column is a plain header holding bare filenames, which does not satisfy the merge image-column contract, so a naive run binds nothing while every badge still shows a picture. And the longest role line runs to more than sixty characters where the median is under thirty, which oversets the badge's fixed role frame at true trim while every other record sits comfortably. Nothing anywhere reports overset.

assets_supplied.name: venue_render.jpg
assets_supplied.visible_description: "The architect's render of the new venue. It is all anyone has because the building has not opened."
assets_supplied.hidden_defect: It is a CGI render with a synthetic sky and impossible interior light, and it will never sit beside photographic portraits on the same page, which is only obvious once the two are actually adjacent. It is also 1,400px on the long edge, so it could not carry a programme opener even if it belonged there.

assets_supplied.name: summit_brand_notes.txt
assets_supplied.visible_description: The summit's house ground description in plain language, the tone words (understated, credible, quiet, professional), the three shapes actually used, and the standing rule that speaker role lines print as contracted.

assets_supplied.name: programme_copy.txt
assets_supplied.visible_description: The programme opener copy, the session track names and the announcement wording the summit posts when a speaker is confirmed.

acceptance_bar: The eighteen read as one event when laid out in the programme grid: one house ground, one treatment, one scale of head in frame. A portrait that cannot be brought to the set is named to us, not shipped at eighty percent.
Nobody is made to look like a different person, and no portrait carries a visible retouching signature. Anything that arrived already heavily worked is named in the note with what you did about it.
All three shapes are delivered for every person, plus a no-ground version for the stage screens whose edge holds when placed over dark video and not only over white.
No invented pixels anywhere. No delivered file exceeds its source, no crop reports an upscale, and where material had to be added at an edge the note says which portraits and why.
Where material was added at an edge, the added band matches that portrait's own ground and the house treatment, judged with the wide shapes laid out together rather than one at a time.
The badge run produces exactly one badge per confirmed person, with the picture on each badge being that person's picture and the head sitting in the frame the way it does on every other badge.
Every field is present on every badge, and no name, role line or affiliation is clipped at true trim. Any badge you cannot give us that way, name it before the file goes to the printer.
Role lines print exactly as the speakers wrote them, not shortened, re-spaced or abbreviated.
Each per-person badge file contains the person its filename claims, established by opening it.
Printer proofs render at real print resolution at badge trim.
All three canvases sit in ONE editable file, each keeping its own canvas size, and we get the self-contained source it was built from.
Any diagram on the programme opener is real editable artwork in that file, not a picture of a diagram.
One type system across all three canvases, with the note naming per role the family, its foundry or designer, and the weight actually used.
The board carries every finished portrait with nothing silently missing from it.
The note states, per portrait, what you did to it, and lists every row in the speaker export you questioned and what was done about it.

adobe_surfaces.role: Brings eighteen self-submitted portraits shot in eighteen rooms to one credible house treatment with one scale of head in frame, decides what to do with frames that arrived already retouched, puts every sitter on the summit's house ground and produces the ground-free versions the stage screens need, derives the three delivery shapes with crop discipline, and adds edge material on the frames that are too tight rather than interpolating them, then brings that added material into the house treatment. It is also the only place the architect's render can be judged against real photography.

It is also where a prepared crop stops being an abstraction and meets a frame whose proportion nobody chose.

The recommender refuses to pair so the pairing is the freelancer's art direction and has to read as a serious professional summit rather than a consumer conference. trajectory.action: Confirm the account tier, pull the authoring playbook, and split the commission: badges to the merge surface, the three canvases to HTML authoring, portraits to imaging.
trajectory.judgement: The brief does not state the split, and it explicitly rules out web pages, which is a constraint on scope rather than on surface. Badges are record per page against artwork the summit wants kept; the three canvases need three sizes and weekly edits.
trajectory.produces: A plan naming deliverable to surface, and the confirmed tier.

trajectory.action: Upload all eighteen portraits, the badge PDF, the export and the render, holding a role manifest.
trajectory.judgement: Handoff discipline. Source dimensions are recorded here because they are the reference every no-upscale claim is made against later.
trajectory.produces: A manifest of presigned URLs with source dimensions per portrait.

trajectory.action: Preview all eighteen and triage: light, ground, tilt, how much room there is above the head, how large the head sits in frame, and which frames arrived already worked on.
trajectory.judgement: Three things have to be decided by looking, not by reading a filename: which frames are too tight for the wide shape before any crop policy is fixed, which frames arrived retouched and therefore need a different destination from the rest, and what one scale of head in frame means across sitters photographed at wildly different distances.
trajectory.produces: A per-portrait triage note and the house treatment target chosen from the strongest frame.

trajectory.action: Straighten what needs it, then correct every portrait toward the house treatment one call per frame, recording parameters.
trajectory.judgement: A batched call applies one identical parameter set, which is exactly wrong across eighteen rooms. The target is a set, and the two already-retouched frames need a decision rather than a correction: pushing them toward the house treatment is the move that makes them worse.
trajectory.produces: Eighteen corrected masters with a per-portrait parameter log and a stated decision on the retouched pair.

trajectory.action: Put every sitter on the summit's house ground, triaging the route per portrait, and produce the ground-free versions for the stage screens.
trajectory.judgement: The one-call ground route and the select-invert-fill route are not interchangeable and the choice is per portrait. Hair against a busy or similar-valued room is where the difference shows, and it shows on dark video rather than on the house ground.
trajectory.produces: House-ground portraits and ground-free portraits for all eighteen.

trajectory.action: Derive the programme shape, the tight square and the wide stage shape for every person, reading each crop's confidence and tradeoff metadata rather than trusting success.
trajectory.judgement: The tradeoffs array is the only signal that a crop clipped, that detection was weak, or that an output was interpolated, and a subject-aware crop on a sparse frame can mis-detect and still report success.
trajectory.produces: Three shapes per person, with a resize and confidence record.

trajectory.action: On the frames too tight for the wide shape, add material at the short edges first and then crop, bringing the added band into the house treatment.
trajectory.judgement: Adding edge material is the only route that does not invent pixels inside the picture, but it introduces synthesised ground that has to match that sitter's own ground and the house treatment, and it is the single sanctioned generative call so it must not be reached for casually.
trajectory.produces: Wide-shape masters for the tight frames without interpolation.

trajectory.action: Lay all eighteen wide shapes out together and look at them as the stage set they will be.
trajectory.judgement: Judging the set as a set at the only moment the comparison exists. Grounds and treatments that agree in isolation can disagree in a row.
trajectory.produces: A set-level verdict on the wide shapes.

trajectory.surface: Data preparation and Creative Cloud storage
trajectory.action: Reconcile the registration export against the confirmed eighteen, normalise headers, build the prefixed image column holding bare filenames, upload the badge-shape portraits and build the image map against them.
trajectory.judgement: Two people appear twice with different affiliations, and choosing which affiliation prints is a decision about somebody's professional identity, not a data-cleaning detail. The image column contract is specific and a plain header binds nothing while every badge still shows a picture.
trajectory.produces: The merge data file, uploaded badge portraits, the image map, and a first list of data questions.

trajectory.action: Convert the badge PDF, export IDML, unzip it, and read the real inventory: frame counts, bounds, object styles, integer page-item ids, and the true story text reconstructed from the content runs.
trajectory.judgement: The binding strategy belongs to the printer's artwork rather than to the plan, and the agent has to establish what is addressable, and at what proportion, before promising anything. It also has to decide which text it computes offsets from.
trajectory.produces: The converted document, its IDML, a real frame inventory with bounds, and a reconstructed story text.

trajectory.action: Author the mapping covering the name, role line, affiliation and the picture frame, and pass it back through the validator.
trajectory.judgement: Choosing the right action for the granularity that came back, using integer page-item ids, ordering same-story rows against the original text, and passing the whole mapping as one stringified object.

trajectory.action: Prepare the merge template, then round-trip IDML from the result and grep for every placeholder the mapping claimed to create.
trajectory.judgement: A success message is not evidence, and nothing in the chain instructs this check.
trajectory.produces: A template whose placeholder inventory has been independently confirmed.

trajectory.action: Merge to a native document with the per-row portraits bound, render the print-resolution proofs, and look at the proofs.
trajectory.judgement: Merging to the native document first keeps the press branch and the per-record branch open and is the only route to real resolution. Looking at what came out, rather than at the success message, is the whole point of this step.
trajectory.produces: The merged document and the first print-resolution proofs, inspected.

trajectory.action: Produce the press file and the per-person badge files by the route whose record identity is guaranteed, naming each by opening it.
trajectory.judgement: Returned order is not trustworthy on every route, and naming eighteen files by position ends with registration reprinting the wrong person's badge.
trajectory.produces: The press badge file and eighteen per-person files, named and identity verified.

trajectory.action: Read every badge at true trim against the speaker export, field by field.
trajectory.judgement: Reading the output rather than the log. Clipped copy is reported nowhere and does not read as clipped at proof scale.
trajectory.produces: A badge by badge reconciliation against the export.

trajectory.action: Search Stock with short generic queries for a real photograph for the programme opener, filter to photography, exclude generative results, license and download at full resolution, then bring it toward the house treatment and lay it beside the portraits.
trajectory.judgement: The architect's render is the obvious free answer and it is the wrong one, which is a judgement about how a render sits beside photography rather than about the render's quality. The licensed frame then has to sit with eighteen portraits rather than merely be good.
trajectory.produces: One licensed camera-scale frame, graded and judged against the set.

trajectory.action: Ask for recommendations once per typographic role, read the family style inventories for real numeric weights, launder every name, and build one kit.
trajectory.judgement: The pairing is the agent's own and has to read as a serious professional summit. Weight cannot be inferred from the style name and the CSS must use the returned stack.
trajectory.produces: A one-kit type system with family, foundry or designer and real weight per role.

trajectory.action: Author one self-contained HTML with three roots at three canvas sizes, embedding every photograph as image data, authoring the session track diagram as inline vector inside an explicitly sized wrapper, and declaring family and weight on every text element. Upload and export, then verify the first canvas by rendition and the other two by parsing the returned markup.
trajectory.judgement: A photograph left as a URL is not a photograph, an auto-sized right-anchored wrapper throws its contents off the canvas, weight is not inherited from markup semantics, and a global canvas override collapses a mixed-size set. Every one of those drops returns success, and the rendition only shows the first canvas.
trajectory.produces: A native editable Express document with three canvases, the retained source, an inspected first canvas and a markup audit of the other two.

trajectory.action: Create the review board and add the finished portraits, batching within the per-call cap and re-sending only entries named as failed. Then write the note.
trajectory.judgement: What to escalate and what to fix silently. The summit asked to be told about the portraits and the data, and the note also has to say plainly that badge typography is the printer's and not the agent's, because the summit will otherwise assume the type system covers it.
trajectory.produces: A persistent shareable board with nothing silently dropped, and the written handover.

emergent_checkpoints.what_can_only_be_learned_by_running: That the badge's picture frame is not the shape the printed badge implies, and that everything bound into it is being re-fitted on the frame's terms. The 2025 badge reads as a square picture chip, so a square badge crop is the reasonable thing to prepare, and the summit's own brief asks for a tight square. The graphic frame behind it is a tall portrait rectangle, and the merge fits whatever is bound into it to that proportion, so the crown of the head is cut on every record. The frame's proportion is geometry inherited from a printer nobody at the summit can ask, it is not visible in the printed artefact, the merge reports success, and each badge looks like a deliberate tight crop when viewed alone. It only declares itself as a fault when the rendered proofs are actually looked at and the same cut appears on all eighteen heads.
emergent_checkpoints.why_unavoidable: (a) Ordering cannot avoid it and care cannot substitute for it. The frame's proportion is not stated in the PDF, is not visible in the printed card, and is not reported by the merge; the only way to it is to convert, read the frame bounds and then bind something and look at what came out. An agent that reads the bounds carefully before binding can catch it one step earlier, which is exactly the competent path this trajectory takes at step 10, and it still cannot know whether the frame fits or fills what is bound into it until a record is actually rendered. (b) Nothing states it. The brief asks for a tight square for badges and avatars, which is the summit describing the shape they use, and the acceptance bar asks that heads sit in the frame the same way on every badge, which is an ordinary client quality requirement. Neither is a disclosure about the artwork's internals. (c) It is not a propagation re-run. The response is to go back to the imaging surface and prepare a different asset: a badge crop at the frame's real proportion with the head placed for that proportion, which is a fresh composition decision per sitter, not the same crop re-fed. The square crop the summit asked for still ships as an avatar deliverable, so the two now diverge.
emergent_checkpoints.likely_rework: Re-derive a badge-specific crop at the picture frame's real proportion for all eighteen, composed for that shape rather than cropped down from the square, re-upload them and rebuild the image map against the new filenames, re-merge and re-render, then read the proofs again on all eighteen rather than on the ones that were changed. Keep the square crop as the avatar deliverable and say in the note that badge and avatar are now two different crops and why, so the summit does not later swap one for the other.
emergent_checkpoints.failure_if_undetected: Eighteen badges go to the printer with the top of every speaker's head cut off, on a run that reported success at every step and looked deliberate on any single badge, for an event whose paying audience reads calibre off exactly this.

emergent_checkpoints.what_can_only_be_learned_by_running: Whether the material added at the edges of the three too-tight frames actually belongs to those pictures. Adding edge material is the only route to the wide stage shape that does not invent pixels inside the picture, but what gets built at the edge is generated from that specific frame's own content: on one sitter it continues the office wall convincingly, on another it invents a lighting falloff that does not match the sitter's own ground, and on a third it produces a band that is plausible in isolation and a full step off the house treatment. None of that is knowable before the operation is run, nothing in the response reports it, and each result looks like a normal photograph on its own. It shows only when the eighteen wide shapes are laid out together as the stage set, where three of them carry a band along one edge that the other fifteen do not.
emergent_checkpoints.why_unavoidable: (a) Ordering cannot dodge it. The expand has to happen after the house treatment is established, since the band has to match that treatment, and it has to happen before the wide crops are final. There is no parameter that guarantees a match and no readout that reports one; the seed parameter makes a result reproducible, not correct. A careful agent doing it right the first time is still handing an outcome to a generative step whose output it has not seen. (b) Nothing states it. The brief says a couple of frames are cropped tightly, which is the client noticing that some pictures are tight, and the acceptance bar requires added material to match, which is the client's standard for the work rather than a warning that it will not. No asset note names which frames or what the band will do. (c) It is not a propagation re-run. The response is a different decision on a different axis: re-run the expand with different amounts or from a different side, correct the band as its own masked region, or abandon expansion for that sitter and accept a looser wide crop that loses the head scale the set is built on, which then changes what one scale of head in frame means for the whole set.
emergent_checkpoints.likely_rework: Re-run the edge material on the frames whose band does not sit, from a different side or at a different extent, and bring the band into the house treatment as a confined correction rather than re-grading the whole frame, which would move the sitter. Where it will not come, choose the looser crop and re-check what that does to the head scale across all eighteen wide shapes, then lay the eighteen out and judge them together again rather than checking only the three that were touched.
emergent_checkpoints.failure_if_undetected: Three of eighteen lower thirds carry a visible band of invented wall along one edge in a different light from the rest, projected at stage scale in front of four hundred people who paid to be there.

emergent_checkpoints.what_can_only_be_learned_by_running: Whether every badge actually holds at true trim. The role lines are the speakers' own contracted titles, supplied by a registration system, and the longest of them is more than twice the median. The role frame's depth is fixed inside a printer's artwork that nobody at the summit can change and that the connector offers no way to resize, reflow or releaded. The two only meet on a typeset badge at real trim size. The failure is silent in every channel: nothing in the merge reports overset, the merge's own raster route renders at screen resolution where a clip does not read as a clip, and the badge looks finished at proof scale.
emergent_checkpoints.why_unavoidable: (a) Neither ordering nor competence produces a fit. The agent cannot shorten the role line, because the summit has said it prints as contracted, and it cannot deepen or reflow the frame, because the mapping surface exposes only text, image and code mappings and no typographic or geometric control whatsoever. Both the constraint and the frame are fixed client property. (b) Nothing states it. The brief says role lines print as written, which is a standard contractual copy clause of the same kind the client already applies to their speakers, and the acceptance bar carries an ordinary quality line about nothing being clipped at trim. Neither says any record is long, and no asset note names the speaker. (c) It is not a propagation re-run, because the input the agent would want to change is the one it is forbidden to touch and the artefact it would want to alter cannot be altered. The checkpoint resolves into a judgement that has to be taken and then made consistent with the earlier decision about the duplicate registrations: either this is a freelancer who quietly edits a client's contractual copy, or one who names in writing what cannot be done inside the client's own artwork.

why_not_vlm: Paste the brief and the assets into a frontier image model and it returns eighteen new faces. IDENTITY is the whole point and the whole prohibition: these are eighteen real speakers whose actual likeness has to survive, and the client says explicitly that nobody may be made to look like a different person. A regenerated headshot on a conference badge is not a design failure, it is a fraud. SPEC: the summit needs one badge per confirmed person at badge trim with contractual role lines bound verbatim, each person's own picture bound per row, eighteen separately named badge files each containing the person its filename claims, print-resolution proofs, and three named crop shapes plus a ground-free version per person. None of that is producible or checkable from a generated image. EDITABILITY: two deliverables are defined by being editable, a live merge template so next year's badges are a data change, and a document the summit restyles weekly as speakers confirm. And the middle of the engagement is verification against material reality: does this frame fit or fill what is bound into it, does this added band match this sitter's ground, does this role line clip at trim, does this edge hold over dark video. None of that is a generation problem.
doability_proof: Five surfaces, honestly counted, every link verified in CONNECTOR_CAPABILITIES_v3 (2026-09-10, auth account). MERGE: the convert, export, generate, prepare, merge, render chain is verified end to end from a bare press PDF, and the badge PDF is specified as a real font-embedding press PDF because thin synthetic PDFs fail conversion opaquely. Per-row image binding is verified visually through a prefixed CSV column plus an image map whose keys match the bare filenames, at three rows, so the eighteen-row run carries an explicit fallback of a recordRange loop binding one image per call, which also guarantees per-record identity. PDF-derived templates are confirmed to contain real image frames when the source PDF places images, and the mapping prompt returns frame bounds, which is the channel the frame-proportion question is answered through. One record per page for PDF output is confirmed, per-record files come from the two order-safe routes, multi-record raster order is documented as reversed and avoided, and 300 ppi comes from document_render_layout because resolution asked for at merge time is silently ignored. The mapping surface exposes only text, image and code mappings with no typographic or geometric control, which is what makes the overset constraint real rather than rhetorical. IMAGING: auto_straighten, auto_tone, masked and unmasked adjustments, select_by_prompt and select_subject with returnBbox, invert_selection, fill_area, remove_background in both transparent and backgroundColor forms, crop_to_bounds, crop_and_resize with its tradeoffs and detection-confidence metadata, and generative_expand are all verified headless. generative_expand is the single sanctioned generative call and is documented as adding pixels only at the edges with AI-generated content and an optional seed, which is exactly how it is used here. crop_and_resize is documented as interpolating to a hard cap and reporting it only in tradeoffs, and subject-aware extraction is documented as silently mis-cropping on sparse art with a low confidence value, so both are scored as decision plus disclosure rather than measurement. Alpha survives crops at png output, which is what the ground-free deliverable depends on. EXPRESS: mixed canvas sizes in one export are verified, inline SVG becomes native editable vector so the track diagram is a real deliverable, external image URLs render as empty placeholders so every photograph is embedded, and the HTML is routed through the text/html upload path because embedded photography exceeds the inline threshold. The rendition preview shows the first canvas only, so canvases two and three are audited from the returned markup. Persistence is not assumed, so the deliverable is the document plus the source. FONTS: the recommend, styles, find, kit chain is verified end to end, and the documented absence of any font file download is why the note must state that badge typography stays the printer's. STOCK AND BOARDS: short queries only, orientation filter never passed, licensing returns camera-scale imagery, boards persist with a twelve-placement cap where 201 means partial success with a failed-items list, so the eighteen-portrait board is sent in two batches. VOLUME: twenty client image files in, roughly forty-eight image artefacts moved in total across three shapes plus ground-free versions, every multi-image call at or under ten and no batch above twenty. AVOIDED: no video or audio, no vector render or vector merge, no variable QR, no bleed gate, no pdfPreset, no fill_text, no animate_design, no replace_image, no download_design, no upscaling, no OCR, no compositing, no generated faces, and no photograph reaching Express as a URL.
